summary: Describes how to prepare, enforce and compare Unicode strings that serve as nicknames, display names or petnames for people, devices, accounts and websites. It was replaced by RFC 8266.

eli5.summary: People pick friendly names with letters from many languages, and this explains how to treat them fairly. It was replaced by RFC 8266.

questions: what is the precis nickname profile
why do nicknames need special rules
subtitle: Standards for preparing and comparing international display names.

tldr.problem: Chat systems, messaging apps, and other services let people choose memorable names in many languages, but comparing and normalizing these international nicknames is complex and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7700 defines the PRECIS Nickname profile: rules for mapping Unicode characters (spaces, case), normalizing them to a standard form, and comparing them so that visually similar names are treated as equivalent.
tldr.outcome: Applications can accept nicknames from users worldwide and reliably compare them, reducing confusion from alternative spellings or character variations. RFC 8266 later updated this profile.

today: RFC 7700 defined the PRECIS Nickname profile and was obsoleted by RFC 8266, which made updates to the profile based on experience with international deployments.

sections.title: What Are Nicknames
sections.content:
A nickname is a memorable, human-friendly name chosen by a person or assigned to an entity. They appear everywhere: as chat room usernames in IRC or XMPP, as display names in email, as labels for devices in a network visualization, and as contact names in address books. Unlike formal identifiers (such as account numbers or SIP URIs), nicknames are meant to be easy to remember and recognize.

When applications support Unicode characters, users can choose nicknames in any language: Greek, Arabic, Chinese, emoji, or mixed scripts. This brings flexibility, but it also introduces complexity. Two users might choose what looks like the same name using different Unicode characters, leading to confusion or unintended duplication.
sections.eli5: A nickname is a friendly name you give yourself or something else, like your username in a chat room. People in different countries like to use letters from their own languages.

sections.title: The PRECIS Framework
sections.content:
RFC 7700 defines a PRECIS Nickname profile built on top of the PRECIS framework (defined in RFC 7564), which is a set of rules for preparing and comparing international strings in application protocols. PRECIS stands for Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings.

The Nickname profile is based on the PRECIS FreeformClass, which permits a wide range of Unicode characters including letters, numbers, symbols, and punctuation. This openness allows nicknames to be creative and expressive. The profile then adds specific rules to handle spaces, case, and character normalization so that nicknames can be reliably compared.
sections.eli5: PRECIS is a set of rules that help computers understand Unicode text in a consistent way. The Nickname profile is a specific recipe from those rules, designed just for nicknames.

sections.title: Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison
sections.content:
RFC 7700 defines three operations on nicknames, each applying a sequence of rules:

Preparation is the first step. The nickname must consist only of characters allowed in the FreeformClass, and it must be encoded as UTF-8.

Enforcement happens when a nickname is submitted. The system applies three mapping rules in order: (1) map any non-ASCII space character (such as thin spaces or hair spaces) to a regular ASCII space; (2) strip spaces from the beginning and end, and collapse interior sequences of multiple spaces into one; (3) apply Unicode Default Case Folding to normalize uppercase and titlecase letters to lowercase. Then the string is normalized using Unicode NFKC (Normalization Form Compatibility Composition), which decomposes and recomposes characters to a standard form. Finally, the system checks that the result is not empty.

Comparison happens when two nicknames need to be checked for equivalence. Both strings are prepared and enforcement rules are applied in order, then two strings are considered the same if they are an exact byte-for-byte match. There is no directionality rule; nicknames can be displayed differently depending on the layout direction of the interface.
sections.eli5: When you type a nickname, the computer cleans it up: it fixes spaces, makes uppercase letters lowercase, and rearranges accents and special marks. Then if two nicknames look the same after cleanup, the computer treats them as the same name.

sections.title: Examples of Normalization
sections.content:
The RFC gives concrete examples of how the rules work. The nickname <Foo> becomes <foo> after case folding. The name <Foo Bar> (with a space) becomes <foo bar>. Interior spacing like <St Peter> (two spaces) gets collapsed to <st peter> (one space).

Two important examples show how Unicode normalization handles characters that look alike. The Greek capital sigma (U+03A3) and the final sigma (U+03C2) both become the small sigma (U+03C3) after case folding. The Roman numeral four (U+2163) becomes the letters <iv> after NFKC normalization. These transformations help prevent confusion when users see similar characters.
sections.eli5: The computer changes HELLO to hello, fixes hello world to hello world, and recognizes that Greek letters Σ and ς are both the same sigma when compared.

sections.title: Security and Visual Similarity
sections.content:
The mapping and normalization rules help reduce confusion from similar-looking characters, but they are not a complete defense against spoofing. The RFC acknowledges that characters can look visually identical or nearly identical to humans but differ in Unicode encoding. An application might see <rn> (the letters r and n) and <m> (the letter m) as different strings, but they appear the same in some fonts.

The RFC delegates detailed security recommendations to other standards: RFC 7564 (PRECIS) covers spoofing risks, and Unicode Technical Standard 39 covers security mechanisms for Unicode. Applications that use the Nickname profile are encouraged to implement additional safeguards, such as restricting character ranges, limiting visually confusable characters, or preventing certain reserved nicknames.
sections.eli5: The cleanup rules help, but they are not perfect. Some letters look almost identical to humans but the computer sees them as different. Applications need to add extra checks if security matters.
